lead: A factor of safety is a number that turns a measured strength into a stress you allow. It covers estimated loads, scattered material properties and the high cost of failure. Design codes are the rulebooks that fix the minimum value and the method. Together they let two engineers size the same part and get the same defensible answer.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.2 for yield strength, ultimate strength and endurance limit, because a factor of safety means nothing until you know which strength you divide.

blocks.text: The factor of safety, symbol n, is a dimensionless number greater than 1. A material strength is divided by it to get the stress permitted in service.
n = S / σ_allow    and    σ_actual ≤ σ_allow
blocks.where: n is the factor of safety (no unit, n > 1); S is the strength for the failure mode, in MPa; σ_allow is the allowable stress, in MPa; σ_actual is the stress from the working load, in MPa. Rearranged, σ_allow = S/n. The check means the actual factor of safety S/σ_actual must be at least the required n.

blocks.text: The strength S depends on the failure mode:

items: Yield strength S<sub>y</sub> for a ductile part that would bend permanently; usual for steel machine members.
Ultimate strength S<sub>ut</sub> for a brittle part that would break without warning, such as a cast-iron bracket.
Endurance limit S<sub>e</sub> for many cycles; fatigue criteria come in Unit 2.

blocks.text: Three uncertainties justify n: the working load is estimated, the strength varies between batches, and failure costs far more than extra material.

items: Pick the strength S for the failure mode.
Compute σ_actual from the working load and geometry (Chapter 1.6).
Choose the required n from a code, or from judgement.
Compare σ_actual with σ_allow; if it fails, enlarge the section or change material.

blocks.text: Margin is n − 1 as a fraction of working stress. n = 2.5 is a 150 per cent margin, not 250 per cent.

sections.h3: Reading a sensible value of n

blocks.text: A single n hides three worries, roughly multiplied:

items: Load uncertainty: steady duty or starting torque, wind, dropped load? Use 1.2 to 1.5.
Material uncertainty: rolled bar is more predictable than a local casting. Use 1.1 to 1.3 for steel, more for cast iron.
Consequence of failure: a farm cart axle and an aircraft part differ. Use 1.1 to 1.5, far more where people are at risk.

blocks.text: Textbook values follow. Steady ductile steel: n = 1.5 to 2 on yield. Impact: 3 or more. Brittle material: 3 to 4 on ultimate. Lifting equipment and pressure vessels: fixed by code, often 4 or higher.
A higher n is not free: it means a heavier, costlier part and more bearing load. The right n is the smallest that covers the real uncertainty.

sections.h3: Design codes are not the same as a factor of safety

blocks.text: A design code is a published document of mandatory rules: load cases, strength values, stress method, minimum n or partial factors, tests and marking. Examples are the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, ISO standards and the Indian Standards of the Bureau of Indian Standards. A code is followed because law, contract or a regulator requires it.
The confusion to avoid: n is a number, a code is a document. A code may fix n, or replace one global n with two factors:

blocks.where: φ (phi) is the resistance factor, ≤ 1, reducing the nominal resistance R (in kN or MPa); γ (gamma) is a load factor, ≥ 1, increasing each nominal load effect Q. The left side is the design strength, the right side the design load effect.

blocks.text: Modern limit-state codes split the margin because loads and strengths have different statistics; a dead load is more predictable than wind or live load. The price is that no single number describes safety.
Codes are a minimum, lag new materials, and cover only written failure modes. A code-compliant part can still fail by fatigue, corrosion or misuse. The code is the floor, not the ceiling.

figure.caption: Two separate branches: the load gives an actual stress, the strength divided by n gives an allowable stress. With these numbers 180 MPa exceeds 112 MPa, so the tie fails.

spec.aria: The load branch gives an actual stress of 180 megapascals from 45 kilonewtons on 250 square millimetres. The strength branch gives an allowable stress of 112 megapascals from a yield strength of 280 megapascals divided by a factor of safety of 2.5. Comparing them, 180 is greater than 112, so the design fails.

nodes.label: Load branch
nodes.note: F = 45 kN on A = 250 mm² → σ_actual = 180 MPa

examples.question: A ductile steel tie has a cross-section of 250 mm² and carries an expected tensile load of 45 kN. The yield strength is 280 MPa. Using n = 2.5 on yield, find (a) the allowable stress, (b) the actual stress, (c) the ratio of actual stress to allowable stress. State whether the design is safe, and find the minimum cross-section that would make it safe.
steps: Use consistent units: 1 MPa = 1 N/mm². Load F = 45 kN = 45 000 N.
Ratio > 1, so not safe. Actual factor of safety = 280 / 180 = 1.56, below 2.5.
Required area A = F / σ_allow = 45 000 / 112 = 401.8 mm². A 20 mm rod gives 314 mm², too small; a 25 mm rod gives 491 mm², which passes.
examples.answer: Allowable stress 112 MPa, actual stress 180 MPa, ratio 1.61, so not safe; it needs at least 402 mm², for example a 25 mm diameter rod.
examples.check:
Sy = 280.0
F = 45e3
A = 250.0
n = 2.5
sigma_allow = Sy / n
sigma_act = F / A
ratio = sigma_act / sigma_allow
A_req = F / sigma_allow
print(round(sigma_allow, 2))
print(round(sigma_act, 2))
print(round(ratio, 2))
print(round(A_req, 2))

examples.question: A cast-iron bracket has S<sub>ut</sub> = 300 MPa. The code requires n = 4 on ultimate. The working stress is 60 MPa. Check the design and find the actual factor of safety.
steps: Compare: working stress 60 MPa ≤ 75 MPa, so safe.
Actual factor of safety = S<sub>ut</sub> / working stress = 300 / 60 = 5.
examples.answer: Allowable stress 75 MPa; working stress 60 MPa is below it, so safe; actual factor of safety 5.
examples.check:
Sut = 300.0
n = 4.0
sigma_work = 60.0
sigma_allow = Sut / n
FoS_actual = Sut / sigma_work
print(round(sigma_allow, 2))
print(round(FoS_actual, 2))

traps: Using S<sub>ut</sub> where yielding governs. A ductile tie that stretches at 280 MPa is not saved by S<sub>ut</sub> = 450 MPa; use S<sub>y</sub>.
Mixing kN and MPa. 1 MPa = 1 N/mm²; convert load to newtons: 45 000 N / 250 mm² = 180 MPa, not 0.18 MPa.
Forcing one n into a limit-state code with φ ≤ 1 and γ ≥ 1; it cannot reproduce the split.
Assuming code compliance means safety; fatigue, corrosion and misuse may be outside the code.
Confusing n with margin: n = 2.5 is a margin of 1.5, or 150 per cent.

quiz.q: Define factor of safety and write it in terms of strength and allowable stress.
quiz.a: n = S / σ_allow, where S is the strength for the failure mode (MPa), σ_allow the allowable stress (MPa), and n a dimensionless number greater than 1.

quiz.q: Why is a larger factor of safety used for a cast-iron bracket than for a rolled-steel tie under the same steady load?
quiz.a: Cast iron is brittle: it fractures without yielding, so no warning and no stress redistribution, and its strength scatters more. Rolled steel yields first with warning and has repeatable properties, so a smaller margin suffices.

quiz.q: A brittle part is made of a material with S<sub>ut</sub> = 420 MPa. The code requires n = 4 on ultimate. Find the allowable stress.
A tie of area 300 mm² carries 60 kN. The material has S<sub>y</sub> = 250 MPa and the required factor of safety is 2.5. Check the design.
quiz.a: σ_actual = 60 000 / 300 = 200 MPa. σ_allow = 250 / 2.5 = 100 MPa. Since 200 > 100, the design is not safe. The actual factor of safety is 250 / 200 = 1.25 against a required 2.5.

quiz.q: A designer uses n = 2 on S<sub>ut</sub> for a mild-steel shaft that would actually fail by yielding. State the error and its effect on the design.
quiz.a: The wrong strength was used. S<sub>ut</sub> is larger than S<sub>y</sub>, so S<sub>ut</sub>/2 is higher than the intended S<sub>y</sub>/2. The shaft yields at a lower load than intended. The allowable exceeds S<sub>y</sub> only when S<sub>ut</sub>/S<sub>y</sub> > n, which is not true for mild steel at n = 2.

quiz.q: Give two differences between a factor of safety and a design code.
quiz.a: n is a single dimensionless number; a code is a published document. A code fixes minimum n or partial factors plus load cases, strength values and method. A code binds through law or contract; n is chosen by the designer.

quiz.q: Why do modern codes split the margin into a load factor above 1 and a resistance factor below 1, instead of using one factor of safety?
quiz.a: Loads and strengths have separate uncertainties and statistics. Splitting lets each be calibrated against measured data, gives different margins to predictable dead load and scattered wind or live load, and keeps reliability consistent across materials. One global n cannot do this.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry has moved to reliability-based design: loads and resistances are random variables with mean and standard deviation, and safety is measured by a reliability index β. Codes calibrate partial factors from measured data. ISO 2394 gives the general principles.
